title: Heater blows cold air
h1: Why is my car heater blowing cold air?
metaDesc: Car heater blowing cold or lukewarm air? Answer a few questions to see if it's low coolant, the thermostat, a blend door or the heater core, and how urgent it is.
synonyms: heater works when driving but not idling
heater stopped working after coolant change
intro: Your car's heat comes from hot engine coolant flowing through a small radiator behind the dash, called the heater core. So a cold heater can be a harmless door problem, or an early warning that the engine is low on coolant. Checking the temperature gauge first tells you which.
safety: If the temperature gauge is in the red or a temperature warning comes on, pull over safely and turn the engine off.
Never open the radiator cap or coolant tank cap on a hot engine. Hot coolant under pressure can cause serious burns.
If you can't clear frost or fog from the windshield, don't drive until you can see clearly.

q_temp_gauge.q: Once the engine has run for 10-15 minutes, where is the temperature gauge?
q_temp_gauge.help: On most cars the needle sits near the middle once warm. Some cars have only a light: blue means still cold, red means too hot.

opts.a: Higher than normal or in the red, or a temperature warning is on
It stays low, near cold, and never reaches the middle
My car has no gauge / I'm not sure

q_coolant.q: With the engine cold, where is the coolant level in the see-through overflow tank?
q_coolant.help: The overflow tank is a plastic bottle near the radiator with MIN and MAX (or COLD and FULL) marks. Only check it when the engine is cold.

opts.a: I haven't checked / I'm not sure

q_inside_signs.q: Do you notice any of these inside the car?

opts.a: A sweet, syrupy smell, a greasy fog on the inside of the windshield, or a damp passenger floor

q_air_behavior.q: The coolant is full. Which of these fits best?

opts.a: It started right after the coolant was changed or the cooling system was repaired
It's warm while driving but goes cold at idle
One side (driver or passenger) is hot and the other is cold
I hear clicking or tapping behind the dash when I change the temperature
It's cold or barely warm all the time, with no other clues

result.title: The engine may be running hot, with coolant not reaching the heater
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe, turn the engine off and let it cool for at least 30 minutes. Then have it towed or call a mobile mechanic.
if: If you can't pull over right away, turn the A/C off and keep the heater on full hot. Even a little heat it gives off helps the engine.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the engine knocks, pull over as soon as it's safe and shut it off right away.
If you see steam or smoke, step away from the car and don't open the hood until it has cooled.
Don't add coolant and carry on to see if it settles. An engine that has overheated needs checking before it's used again.
result.why: A cold heater combined with a high temperature gauge is a common sign that coolant is very low or isn't circulating. The heater core goes cold first because it sits at the end of the line. Without enough coolant, the engine can overheat badly in minutes.

causes.name: Very low coolant from a leak
causes.clues: A sweet smell, steam, drips, or an empty overflow tank once cool.

causes.name: Failed water pump
causes.clues: A grinding or whining noise near the belt, or coolant dripping from that area.

causes.name: Thermostat stuck closed
causes.clues: The gauge climbs quickly after starting, even with full coolant.

causes.name: Head gasket leak
causes.clues: White sweet-smelling exhaust smoke or bubbles in the coolant tank.

you: Once fully cool, check the overflow tank and look under the car for drips.

result.title: The thermostat may be stuck open, so the engine never fully warms up
result.now: Book a check when convenient. A shop will usually confirm with live temperature data before replacing the thermostat. Until then, make sure your windshield can still be cleared before you drive.
if: If the windshield won't defrost, don't drive until it's clear. Get it fixed sooner in cold weather.
If the gauge reads low but the engine actually feels hot, the temperature sensor or gauge may be at fault instead.
If the gauge ever swings high or a temperature warning comes on, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
result.why: The thermostat keeps coolant in the engine until it reaches working temperature. If it's stuck open, coolant flows through the radiator all the time, so the engine stays cool and so does your heater, especially on the highway and in cold weather. It also hurts fuel economy.

causes.name: Thermostat stuck open
causes.clues: The gauge stays low, especially at highway speed, and heat is weak on cold days.

causes.name: Faulty temperature sensor
causes.clues: The gauge reads cold even after a long drive, but the engine feels hot.

causes.name: Cooling fan running constantly
causes.clues: The fan runs even when the engine is cold.

you: Note how long the gauge takes to move off cold on a cold day.
shop: Code scan and live temperature data

result.title: Check the coolant level first
result.now: With the engine fully cold, check the overflow tank. If it's below MIN, top it up to MAX with the coolant type in your owner's manual and see whether the heat returns.
if: If the level was low, the coolant went somewhere. Have the leak found within a few days.
If the temperature gauge rises above normal, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the coolant is full and the heat is still cold, a blend door or clogged heater core is more likely.
If you see steam, smell coolant inside the car or the windshield fogs with a greasy film, don't keep driving. Have it checked first.
result.why: Low coolant is one of the most common reasons a heater goes cold, because the heater core is one of the first places to lose hot coolant when the level drops. It's quick and safe to check when the engine is cold.

causes.name: Low coolant
causes.clues: The tank is below MIN.

causes.name: Blend door problem
causes.clues: The coolant is full, and you hear clicking behind the dash.

causes.name: Clogged heater core
causes.clues: The coolant is full and the engine warms normally, but heat stays weak.

you: Check the overflow tank when cold.
Watch the temperature gauge on your next drive.

result.title: The heater core may be leaking inside the car
result.now: Top up the coolant when the engine is cold, and get the heater core checked within the next few days.
if: If the windshield fogs up so you can't see, don't drive it until it's fixed.
If the temperature gauge rises above normal, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the coolant drops quickly, have it towed rather than keep refilling it.
result.why: The heater core sits behind the dash. When it leaks, hot coolant turns to vapor in the cabin, leaving a sweet smell and an oily fog on the glass, and it can soak the passenger carpet. Coolant vapor isn't something to breathe for long, and the fogging can block your view.

causes.name: Leaking heater core
causes.clues: A sweet smell inside, greasy fog on the windshield, or a wet passenger floor.

causes.name: Leaking heater hose connection behind the dash
causes.clues: The same signs, but the leak is near where the hoses pass through to the cabin.

causes.name: Water leak from the A/C drain or a seal
causes.clues: The wet floor is clear, with no smell, and it's worse after rain or A/C use.
causes.against: If the liquid is clear and odorless, coolant is unlikely.

you: Press a paper towel into the wet carpet and check for color and a sweet smell.
Wipe the inside of the windshield and see whether it leaves a greasy film.

result.title: Low coolant is a likely reason there's no heat
result.now: With the engine cold, top up the overflow tank to MAX with the right coolant, then have the leak found within the next few days. Until then, keep trips short and watch the temperature gauge.
if: If the temperature gauge rises above normal, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the level drops again within a day or two, have it towed rather than keep driving.
If you see white sweet-smelling exhaust smoke or milky oil, don't drive it.
If the overflow tank was completely empty, the engine itself may be low too. Have it checked before driving rather than just refilling the tank.
result.why: When coolant is low, the heater core loses its supply of hot coolant first, so a cold heater is often the earliest warning. The engine can overheat next, so the leak needs finding.

causes.name: External leak (hose, radiator, water pump)
causes.clues: Drips under the front of the car, or crusty colored deposits.

causes.name: Worn radiator or tank cap
causes.clues: Residue around the cap.

causes.name: Internal leak (head gasket)
causes.clues: No visible leak, white exhaust smoke or milky oil.

you: Top up and mark the level, then check it each morning.
Put cardboard under the engine overnight to spot drips.
shop: Combustion gas (block) test if no leak is found

result.title: Air may be trapped in the cooling system
result.now: Have the shop that did the work bleed the air out of the cooling system within the next few days. Watch the temperature gauge closely until then.
if: If the gauge rises above normal, pull over and turn the engine off.
If you hear gurgling behind the dash, that's a sign of trapped air.
If you see steam or the coolant level keeps dropping, stop driving it and have it checked.
result.why: After coolant is drained or refilled, air can get trapped in the high points of the system, including the heater core. The air blocks hot coolant from reaching the heater, and a large air pocket can also cause overheating.

causes.name: Air trapped after coolant service
causes.clues: It started right after a coolant change or repair, and you may hear gurgling.

causes.name: Coolant level dropped as air worked out
causes.clues: The overflow tank level fell after the first few drives.

causes.name: New leak from the repair
causes.clues: Drips or wet spots near the parts that were worked on.

you: Check the overflow tank level when cold after each of the next few drives.
Listen for gurgling behind the dash at startup.

result.title: Coolant flow is weak at low engine speed
result.now: Check the coolant level when cold, and get the cooling system checked within the next few days.
if: If the temperature gauge rises at idle too, avoid traffic and pull over and turn the engine off if it nears the red.
If you hear grinding near the engine belt, the water pump may be failing. Don't drive it.
If you see steam or smell coolant, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
result.why: At idle, the water pump turns slowly and pushes less coolant. If the coolant is slightly low, there's an air pocket, or the pump or heater core is partly restricted, there isn't enough flow to keep the heater warm until the engine speeds up.

causes.name: Slightly low coolant or trapped air
causes.clues: The level is near MIN, or there's gurgling behind the dash.

causes.name: Partly clogged heater core
causes.clues: Coolant that hasn't been changed in years, or heat that's weak even when driving.

causes.name: Worn water pump
causes.clues: A whine near the belt, or a crusty trail below the pump.

you: Check the coolant level when cold.
Notice whether the heat comes back when you raise the engine speed in Park.

result.title: A blend door or its motor may be stuck
result.now: Try switching the climate control off and on, or turning the car off for a few minutes, then book a check when convenient.
if: If the windshield can't be cleared, don't drive until it's fixed.
If the clicking stops and the heat changes, the actuator may be slipping and could fail completely soon.
result.why: A small door behind the dash blends hot air from the heater core with cold air. A small electric motor moves it. When the motor's gears strip or it loses its position, the door stays on cold, often with a clicking or tapping sound. Cars with separate driver and passenger temperatures have a door for each side.

causes.name: Failed blend door actuator
causes.clues: Clicking or tapping behind the dash, or one side hot and the other cold.

causes.name: Actuator out of calibration
causes.clues: It started after a battery change or dead battery.

causes.name: Climate control panel fault
causes.clues: Buttons or displays also act strangely.

you: Change the temperature setting and listen behind the dash for a motor or clicking.
Compare the air from the driver and passenger vents.
shop: HVAC code scan and actuator test
Heater hose temperature check to rule out a coolant problem

result.title: The heater core may be clogged
result.now: Book a heating system check when convenient. Make sure your windshield can still be cleared in the meantime.
if: If the windshield won't defrost, don't drive until it's clear, and get it fixed sooner.
If the temperature gauge ever rises above normal, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Over the years, old coolant can leave deposits that block the narrow passages in the heater core. The engine warms up normally and the coolant is full, but too little hot coolant gets through to warm the air.

causes.name: Clogged heater core
causes.clues: Coolant that hasn't been changed in a long time, and weak heat that slowly got worse.

causes.name: Stuck blend door
causes.clues: Clicking behind the dash, or a sudden change rather than a slow decline.

causes.name: Stuck heater control valve (some vehicles)
causes.clues: One heater hose is hot and the other stays cool.

you: Note whether the heat faded slowly over months or stopped suddenly.
shop: Blend door and HVAC actuator test
Heater core flush, if testing shows the core is restricted

result.title: Check the coolant, then have the heating system looked at
result.now: Check the coolant level when the engine is cold and book a check when convenient. Make sure you can clear the windshield before driving.
if: If the temperature gauge rises above normal, pull over and turn the engine off.
If you notice a sweet smell inside or a damp passenger floor, get it checked within a few days.
If you see steam, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off.
result.why: If the engine warms up normally and the coolant is full, the cause is usually inside the heating system, like a stuck door or a clogged heater core. A shop can usually tell which by feeling the heater hoses and testing the controls.

causes.name: Blend door problem
causes.clues: Clicking behind the dash, or uneven heat side to side.

causes.name: Clogged heater core
causes.clues: Heat that faded slowly over time.

causes.name: Low coolant or trapped air
causes.clues: Gurgling behind the dash, or recent coolant work.

you: Check the coolant level when cold.
Listen for clicking behind the dash when changing the temperature.
